Introduction

The purpose of this Development Control Plan (DCP) is to support the provisions of the Strathfield Local Environmental Plan 2012 (LEP) by providing more detailed planning and design guidelines to assist in the assessment and determination of development applications within the Strathfield local government area.

This DCP is intended to be read in conjunction with the Strathfield LEP 2012. In the event of any inconsistency between the DCP and the LEP, the provisions of the LEP will prevail, in accordance with the statutory planning requirements.

Compliance with the provisions of this DCP does not guarantee development consent. All Development Applications (DAs) will be assessed on their individual merits, having regard to the Strathfield LEP 2012, this DCP, the relevant considerations outlined unde r Section 4.15 of the Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 , and any other policies adopted by the consent authority.

Savings and Transitional Arrangements

A Development Application (DA) lodged prior to the adoption of this Development Control Plan (DCP) but not yet determined will be assessed in accordance with the provisions that were in force at the time of lodgement. This ensures that applicants are not d isadvantaged by changes to planning controls introduced after their application was submitted.

Structure and Application of This Part of the DCP

The table below establishes the different development types this chapter of the DCP covers, as well as which sections apply within this chapter.

Development TypeSections that apply to development type
Dwelling HousesSections 1 -12
Secondary DwellingsSections 1 -13
Dual OccupanciesSections 1 -12
Multi-Dwelling HousesSections 1 -12
TerracesSections 1 -12
Manor HomesSections 1 -12

This part of the DCP should be read in conjunction with other relevant parts of the overall DCP, including:

  • Part H - Waste Minimisation and Management
  • Part K - Development on Contaminated Land
  • Part N - Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD)
  • Part O - Tree Management
  • Part P - Heritage
  • Part R - Subdivision
  • Part Q - Urban Design Controls

In the event of any inconsistency between this section and other sections of Council's DCP or adopted policies, the provisions of this section shall prevail to the extent of the inconsistency , to ensure clarity and avoid contradiction.

1. Site Analysis

Objectives

O1.1 Development is compatible with the scale, character and landscape setting of the surrounding streetscape and the desired future character of the area .

O1.2 Development adapts to site conditions to allow for retention of significant trees and natural ground levels.

O1.3 Development is appropriately sited and designed to achieve high levels of amenity for future residents and minimise adverse amenity impacts on neighbouring properties .

O1.4 Allotment widths and configurations allow for developments to address the public domain and retain the amenity of the public domain.

Controls

C1.1 Site Analysis Plan

All development proposals involving physical works must include a Site Analysis Plan. New dwellings must address all listed items, while alterations and additions need only address the items relevant to the proposal.

The Site Analysis Plan must show the following:

  • subdivision pattern and pattern of building footprints within all adjoining allotments,
  • topography/site slope,
  • overland flow and flood affectation,
  • orientation of the site,
  • existing vegetation and trees, including street trees,
  • windows and openings on neighbouring buildings,
  • easements,
  • existing retaining walls and boundary fences,
  • driveway locations and vehicular crossovers,
  • existing power poles and public domain alignment,
  • Any significant noise sources,
  • relationship to neighbouring properties, any adjoining heritage items or conservation areas (or any items opposite the site) and any public open spaces or public domain adjoining the site.

C1. 2 Design Verification Statement

Design Verification Statements are required to ensure that Council is provided with a clear rationale for the design approach, and that developments demonstrate a considered and context-sensitive response.

A Design Verification Statement must be prepared by a registered architect for any development comprising three (3) or more dwellings , or any development incorporating a battle-axe access handle, as well as all Co-Living and Boarding House proposals. The D esign Verification Statement must:

  • Demonstrate how the proposal responds to the site constraints, opportunities and context identified in the Site Analysis Plan,
  • Explain how the development integrates with the existing desired and future character, including the surrounding scale, built form and streetscape and its relationship to adjoining sites, and
  • Identify how the design achieves compliance with all relevant development controls and justify any proposed non-compliances.

Note - For Residential Flat Buildings, Mixed Use or Shop Top Housing, the above Design Verification Statement is not required where a Design Verification Statement has been prepared to address requirements in the Environmental Planning and Assessment Regulation (2021) .

C1. 3 Building Orientation

C1 .3.1 Developments are to be designed to maximise the number of dwellings orientated to address the street and/or public domain. Where a dwelling frontage is not orientated towards the street or public domain, it must be demonstrated that this outcome is the result of unique site constraints and that the amenity of the proposed dwelling(s) and any neighbouring dwelling will not be negatively impacted.

C1 .3.2 Dwelling Houses

All dwelling houses must be designed to front the primary road with a clear sense of street address.

Any dwelling house proposed on a rear allotment accessed by a battle -axe must also be orientated towards the street (primary or secondary) and must incorporate a building envelope, building height and façade articulation that responds to the site constrain ts and neighbouring dwellings .

C1 .3.3 Dual Occupancies

  • The optimal configuration for dual occupancies is a 'side by side' attached layout with both dwellings addressing the street.
  • Detached front and back configurations should be limited to allotments with site constraints that demand a unique development response, such as corner sites or sites with dual frontage/rear lane access.
  • Attached 'front and back' and detached 'side by side' dual occupancies are discouraged and expected to be an option for unusual sites and corner allotments only.

C1 .3.4 Multi-Dwelling Housing

  • For a mid-block development, the preferred configuration for multi-dwelling housing is for all dwellings to be orientated to the front primary road, with adequate internal separation between dwellings achieved to ensure private amenity between individual dwellings and adjoining properties.
  • Where dwellings are proposed to be oriented toward a side boundary, the applicant must demonstrate that the optimal street-facing configuration is not achievable and must comply with all setback and other relevant controls outlined in this DCP.

Figure 1 - Ideal mid-block arrangement and orientation for multi-dwelling housing

C1 .3.5 Terraces

All terraces must be designed to front a public road.

C1 .3.6 Manor Homes

  • Manor Homes should be designed to address all road frontages. Individual dwellings should be orientated towards either the street/public road, or to the rear boundary.
  • Aspect to any side boundary should be secondary, with the primary orientation as per control (a) above .

C1.4 Mini mum Frontages

The following minimum frontage widths apply. The width is to be measured along the front boundary line for regular shaped allotments. Where the allotment fans out (or in) so that there is a difference of more than 2m between the front boundary width and the rear boundary width, then the frontage width should be taken from the front setback. Refer to the setback controls for how the front setback is calculated.

C1 .4.1 Dual Occupancies

  • 15m

C1 .4.2 Multi-Dwelling Housing

  • R2 Low Density Residential Zone - 21 m
  • R3 Medium Density Residential Zone - 15 m
  • R4 High Density Residential Zone - 25m

C1 .4.3 Terraces

  • R2 Low Density Residential Zone - 21 m
  • R3 Medium Density Residential Zone - 15m

C1 .4.4 Manor Homes

  • 15m - all zones.

2. Earthworks (Cut and Fill)

Objectives

O2.1 Design development and associated landscaped areas to retain and follow the natural topography of the site.

O2.2 Ensure that excavation and fill does not result in an unreasonable loss of privacy for neighbouring properties.

O2.3 Minimise the impact on overland flow drainage patterns and groundwater intrusion by minimising earthworks across a site.

O2.4 Excavation for basement parking does not impact on landscaping and deep soil requirements.

Controls

C2.1 Excavation and Fill

C2.1 .1 Developments are to avoid unnecessary earthworks by designing and siting to respond to the natural slope of the land and minimise cut and fill . The building footprint must be stepped to respond to the slope of the land and ensure that the ground floor does not sit above 1m from existing ground level at any point.

C2.1. 2 Basements and basement parking areas must be contained within the footprint of the ground floor walls (not including any rear alfresco area). The basement line may cut across any notch or courtyard located along the side elevation of the ground floor, provided those spaces are not identified as contributing to minimum deep soil requirements. Basements and basement parking areas must also not encroach into the side, front or rear setback.

C2.1. 3 Despite C.21.2 above, basements for residential flat buildings over 6 stories may have a basement that extends beyond the ground floor footprint and into the setbacks, provided the relevant deep soil landscaping requirement is achieved.

C2.1. 4 Natural ground level must be maintained within the side setbacks. When earthworks are required to address site irregularities within the side setbacks, cut and fill is limited to 250mm.

C2.1. 5 Development must ensure that fill beneath any structure does not exceed 1000mm. The provision of a basement does not constitute justification for elevated floor levels above this limit, irrespective of flood affectation.

C2.1.6 Natural ground level should be maintained within the front and rear setbacks. To accommodate sudden changes in levels, retaining walls (as part of an integrated and cohesive landscape design) are permitted up to a height of 600mm. Terracing should be utilised where topography requires retaining walls higher than 600mm.

C2.1.7 Earthworks are not to increase or concentrate overland stormwater flow or aggravat e existing flood conditions, on adjacent land.

3. Building Envelope - Setbacks, Height, Building Scale and Building Articulation

Objectives

O3.1 Integrate new development with the existing character of the locality by achieving suitable building separation and consistent bulk and scale.

O3.2 Encourage the breakup and articulation of building facades to provide visual relief, modulation and reduce the overall building bulk.

O3.3 Allow for retention of significant vegetation and provide opportunities for landscape planting, private open space and establishment of tree canopy.

O3.4 Deliver high-quality development which is positioned and orientated to address the street frontage providing a clearly identifiable street entry.

Controls

C3.1 Front Setback

C3.1.1 The minimum front building setback is the average of the existing front setback at the site and the two existing dwellings either side of the site (total of 5 dwellings). Where a site does not have two dwellings either side of the site, the proposal must demonstrate that the proposed setback is consistent with the prevailing street setback in the block.

Note: The setback is to be calculated from the building line being the horizontal distance between the property boundary and:

  • (a) a building wall, or
  • (b) the outside face of any balcony, deck or the like, or
  • (c) the supporting posts of a carport or verandah roof,

whichever distance is the shortest.

Figure 2 - Calculation of the front setback for standard mid -block allotment

C3.1. 2 Council will generally not support a front building setback that is deeper than the prevailing street setback established in Condition 3.1.1 above , unless site constraints require this .

  • C3.1. 3 The front building setback must be free of ancillary structures, such as swimming pools, clothes lines, carports, aboveground rainwater tanks and outbuildings.

C3.2 Side setbacks - All developments

  • C3.2.1 On east-west orientated allotments, the minimum building side setback may need to be increased to ensure that the solar access requirements in this DCP are met for any southern neighbour.
  • C3.2.2 The side setback is calculated from the building line and the property boundary.

C3.3 Side setbacks - Dwellings and Dual Occupancies

  • C3.3.1 The minimum side setback for two (2) storey developments is 1.2m.
  • C3.3.2 Where a third storey is permitted and proposed, additional setbacks must feature in the design to reduce building bulk and scale.

C3.4 Side setbacks - Multi-Dwelling Housing and Terraces

  • C3.4.1 For developments that are fronting the street and are two storeys or less in height, the minimum side setback is 1. 2m.
  • C3.4.2 For a development or a dwelling that is orientated so that the front or rear of the dwelling faces the side boundary, minimum side setback (being the setback between the façade line and the allotment side boundary) are:

In the R2 Low Density zone:

  • 5m to one side boundary including a minimum 3m wide deep soil area with landscaping capable of providing a visual buffer (this deep soil area contributes to achieving overall site targets),
  • 3m to the other side boundary including a 1.5m landscape strip ,
  • Placement of the long side (5m) should consider solar access impacts to any southern neighbour where a site has an east -west orientation.

In the R3 Medium Density zone or any other zone:

  • 4m to one side boundary including a minimum 2m wide deep soil area with landscaping capable of providing a visual buffer (this deep soil area contributes to achieving overall site targets),
  • 2m to the other side boundary including a 1.5m landscape strip ,
  • Placement of the long side (4m) should consider solar access impacts to any southern neighbour where a site has an east -west orientation,

Figure 3 - Setbacks for siding on MDH (row houses) including landscape and deep soil strips

  • C3.4.3 Multi-dwelling housing (t erraces) must comply with the setback at the edge of the development site. Within the development site, a 1. 2m break is required every 6 dwellings. This break should be utilised to provide rear yard access for one of the dwellings.

C3.4.4 Three storey developments must feature an additional 1.5m setback for the second level. With a 1.2m setback for ground and level 1, this would require a 2.7m setback at level 2. High quality alternatives that achieve the effect of the second storey 1.5m setback will be considered on merit.

C3.5 Side Setbacks for Manor Homes

C3.5.1 The minimum side setbacks for manor homes is 1.5m.

C3.5.2 Any living space in a manor homes must also be a minimum of 6m from the building façade of any neighbouring dwelling. This is to ensure adequate building separation for living spaces in apartments.

C3.6 Rear Setbacks - All developments

C3.6.1 For development in the R2 Low Density Residential zone, the minimum rear building setback for all developments is:

  • 10m or 20% of the average length of the site, whichever is lesser ,
  • Not less than 6m.

The rear setback is the distance between the rear boundary and rear building line (irrespective of the developments orientation).

Figure 6 below illustrates how this setback would be applied for Multi-Dwelling Housing developments where dwellings are not orientated to front the street.

Figure 6 - Rear setbacks for Multi-Dwelling Housing with a siding on orientation (50m deep allotment).

C3.6.2 For development in all other zones, the minimum rear building setback is 6m.

C3.7 Internal Setbacks

C3.7.1 Where a development proposes multiple detached dwellings within a site (such as a detached dual occupancy or detached multi-dwelling units), the following building separation requirements apply:

  • Where the dwellings adjoin each other along a side wall (i.e. they are in the same row and not in an attached configuration), a 2.4m building separation is required,
  • Where the dwellings are configured with the side of one dwelling facing the rear of another dwelling, the building separation must be 7.2m (allowing for a rear setback of 6m and side setback of 1.2m),
  • Where the rear of one dwelling faces the front of another dwelling, the building separation must be 10m (allowing for a rear setback of 6m and front setback of 4m).

C3.8 Building Height

  • C3.8.1 The maximum permitted number of storeys at any point for development in the R2 Low Density Residential zone is two (2). Attics are permitted, however only in developments with a pitched roof form.
  • C3.8.2 Where development is proposed on a sloping site, the building is to step to respond to the topography of the site and to ensure the relevant height limit is achieved.
  • C3.8.3 The minimum internal floor to ceiling heights are:
  • For living spaces - 2.7m ,
  • For bedrooms and bathrooms - 2.4m.

C3.9 Attic Design

  • C3.9.1 Attics will be permitted within a development with a pitched roof only. Attics must be designed to:
  • Be integrated into a pitched roof with an angle of between 20° - 30°,
  • Provide natural light and cross ventilation,
  • The extent of Gross Floor Area (GFA) in the attic is to be shown clearly in plan and section drawings.
  • C3.9.2 Dormers in attics along the side and rear elevations must be:
  • no longer than 7m,
  • be setback a minimum 1500mm from the wall line below,
  • must be positioned equidistant within the roofscape,
  • 500mm below the ridgeline .

Figure 7 - Attic Design

  • C3.9.3 Dormers or windows in attics along the front elevation must not consume more than 50% of the roofscape.
  • C3.9.4 Windows in dormers on side and rear elevations are to be designed to minimise any overlooking and privacy impacts to neighbouring properties.

C3.10 Façade Articulation - Front Elevation

  • C3.10 .1 All developments are to be orientated to address the street.
  • C3.10 .2 The front façade of all developments must respond to the public domain and be modulated and articulated. The front façade must incorporate:
  • All front facades must address the street and public domain ,
  • Balconies should feature on upper floors, or other suitable forms of passive surveillance,
  • Windows at all levels that achieve passive surveillance to the street. Sunlight is managed through building recesses and angles and integrated shading devices rather than opaque glazing,
  • Visible ground floor pedestrian entry,
  • Changes in the building line and recesses in the façade through balconies, porches and architectural design features,
  • A composition of varied building materials,
  • The development should be expressed externally through facade features such as party walls and floor slabs,
  • Upper level setbacks at any second or third level.
  • C3.10 .3 Dual occupancies must incorporate a pavilion or similar feature that visually separates the two dwellings. The pavilion design feature must be an integrated part of a cohesive design.

C3.10 .4 The following will not be supported on any development:

  • Obscured glazing on the front façade,
  • Porticos that extend beyond single storey level.

C3.10 .5 For Manor Homes and Multi-Dwelling Housing where site constraints do not allow for all dwellings to be orientated towards the street , a minimum of one (1) dwelling must have direct frontage to the primary road and the façade of that dwelling must be designed to address the public domain.

C3.11 Façade Articulation - Side and Rear Elevation

C3.11 .1 The design of the side and rear elevations should be modulated and articulated and designed to mitigate overlooking into adjoining properties.

C3.11.2 The maximum length of unbroken wall along the side elevation is 15m. To provide modulation and articulation, where a wall length is greater than 15m, the wall is to be articulated by a recess of at least 1m in depth and 2m in length. For 3 storey developments where additional setbacks are required at level 2, this break in the building line must be considered as part of a cohesive design approach that manages bulk and scale.

C3.12 Voids

C3.12 .1 Voids within developments must demonstrate that they provide solar -access benefits, including being positioned to enhance access to natural daylight from a northern aspect. Large voids (>5m²) will only be supported where the design response clearly shows they are necessary to achieve minimum solar -access requirements and/or adequate sunlight penetration .

C3.12 .2 To reduce the overall bulk and scale of a development, stairs and lifts should be located around a single core.

4. Access, Parking and Circulation

Objectives

O4.1 Minimise the visual impact of driveway crossovers, garages and parking areas so they are not visually dominant on the development or in the streetscape.

O4.2 Design and position vehicular access to retain existing street trees and on -street parking.

O4.3 Design car parking, circulation and access to be safe , efficient and minimise the potential for pedestrian and vehicle conflict, and allow ease of access, egress and on -site manoeuvring.

04.4 Developments provide for pedestrian access and entry points that are identifiable from the public domain.

Controls

C4.1 Parking Provision & Garage Design

C4.1 .1 Developments are to achieve the parking rates below.

Dwelling TypeMinimum Parking Spaces Required
Secondary Dwelling0 Spaces required
Dwelling House2 spaces per dwelling
Dual Occupancy1 space per dwelling
Multi-Dwelling Housing, Terraces & Manor Homes (including the residential component of any mixed use or shop top housing development)1 space per dwelling
  • *Note 1 - Where a parking space is proposed for a secondary dwelling, it must not result in an additional driveway crossover from the primary road or non -compliance with any other provision in this DCP such as landscaping requirements. A secondary crossover will be considered for sites with a dual frontage where the second crossover is from the secondary street and will not impact on street trees, other parts of the public domain or the amenity of any neighbour.
  • *Note 2 - Where a basement is proposed for a dwelling house on allotments greater than 750m², there is no maximum on the number of parking spaces provided, provided that the requirements for basement excavation and design are met. The basement parking spaces, and any basement vehicular access, loading areas, garbage and services are excluded from t he calculation of GFA. In this instance, all parking spaces must be located within the basement, and the basement footprint must not extend outside of the building footprint or into the setbacks as prescribed by Council's controls.

*Note 3 - For Manor Homes, parking spaces are to be allocated to apartments on the Architectural Drawings, demonstrating a suitable distribution of parking spaces across the proposed dwellings.

C4.1 .2 All garaging, including any carport must be located at, or behind the front building setback and be designed to be visually recessive and integrated into the design. The permitted widths for garage entry (wall to wall) are:

Dwelling TypeMaximum width
Dwelling House with at-grade garage6m per dwelling
Dwelling house with basement garage3.4m per dwelling
Dual Occupancy (at-grade or basement)3.4m per dwelling (two car spaces to be in a tandem configuration) or 6m when combined (+ the width of any separating wall)
Multi-Dwelling Housing & Terraces with individual dwelling access3.4m per dwelling
Multi-Dwelling Housing and Terraces with combined access to a common parking area and Manor Homes6m. Any variation to this width must be justified in a Traffic and Parking Impact Assessment. The design should endeavour to be the minimum width required for safe access and egress.
  • C4.1 .3 At grade shared parking areas must form an integrated part of the building and landscape regime and have a logical connection to pedestrian entry points. Light coloured materials and/or permeable paving should be used for parking areas and driveways.

C4.1 .4 Garages shall be accessed directly from a rear lane where this is available.

C4.1. 5 Garages and parking areas are to be designed so that electric vehicle and bicycle charging points can be installed as part of the proposal or at a later date. This will include the provision of 3 phase power to car parking areas.

C4.1 .6 Where basement parking is proposed, the basement must be accessed via one driveway and the basement must provide the parking for all dwellings proposed across the development site.

C4.1 .7 Where basement parking is proposed:

  • The basement must allow for forward egress. Turning paths and parking dimensions must be shown on the submitted Architectural Drawings,
  • Basement parking areas must be contained within the footprint of the ground floor walls (not including any rear alfresco area). The basement line may cut across any notch or courtyard located along the side elevation of the ground floor, provided those spaces are not identified as contributing to minimum deep soil requirements . Basements parking areas must also not encroach into the side, front or rear setback ,
  • Driveway access to basement car parking is visually recessive and forms an integrated component of the landscape design for the site,
  • It must not create adverse streetscape impacts due to excessive retaining walls, or entrances that create the appearance of a third storey in areas where development is limited to only two storeys,
  • Parking should be located wholly underground. Where basement parking extends above ground level (existing), it is to be designed to be integrated with the architectural and landscape design of the development,
  • Vehicle entries should be located at the lowest point of the site minimising ramp lengths, excavation and impacts on the building form and layout,
  • Must not result in a ground floor being more than 1000mm above existing ground level. An exceedance of this requirement due to the need to achieve free board requirements for flood affected lots will not be supported by Council.

C4.1.8 Where under-croft parking is proposed:

  • Utilise screening, landscaping, public art integrated into the façade and other methods of building articulation to integrate the parking area into the development,
  • Ensure access to the parking is available from outdoor common areas, as well as individual units.

4.2 Vehicle Access

C4.2.1 Developments shall be designed to minimise the number of driveway crossovers. Traffic and Parking Assessments prepared by suitably qualified engineers are required for variations to driveway crossover widths and for any development proposing >3 dwellings. Maximum crossover numbers and widths for different development types and scena rios are as follows:

Dwelling Type / Development ScenarioMaximum number of crossovers & crossover width
Dwelling House1 single width (3m) crossover per site/development.
Dual Occupancy2 single width (3m each) crossovers (1 per dwelling) or a combined crossover with a maximum width of 5.4m. Where a dual occupancy incorporates a basement garage, access to the basement parking is to be provided via a single crossover and basement ramp no wider than 5.4m.
Single driveway crossovers and access easements will be required for dual occupancies where existing street trees do not allow for two driveway crossovers and separated access.
Multi-Dwelling Housing Terraces with access via the front / primary road and no secondary road running along the rear.For developments with ≥4 dwellings a single point of access must be provided with a maximum width of 5.4m. Narrower crossovers and driveways with traffic signalling may be required where site constraints such as street trees or road conditions require. For developments with <4 dwellings, each dwelling may have individual access from the street. To ensure on- street parking is maximised, two of the crossovers shall be combined into a 5.4m wide combined crossover, with the third incorporating a single width (3m) crossover.
Terraces with rear lane access1 single width (3m) crossover per dwelling.
Manor HomesOne 5.4m wide crossover per development/site . Traffic and Parking Impact Assessment to be submitted justifying the width of the crossover and any circumstance where a second crossover is proposed.

C4.2.2 Vehicle access points and parking areas must:

  • be easily accessible and recognisable to motorists,
  • not disrupt pedestrian flow and safety, and
  • be located to minimise traffic hazards and the potential for vehicles to queue on public roads.

C4.2.3 Driveway crossings are to be positioned so that on-street parking is maximised. A minimum of one on-street parking space is to be retained for every 15m of street frontage where on -street parking currently exists. For sites with a frontage less than 15m in width, one on -street parking space must be retained.

Figure 8 - On-street parking spaces for single dwellings and dual occupancy development

Figure 9 - On-street parking spaces for multi-dwelling housing

C4.2.4 Existing driveways must be used unless the applicant can demonstrate that:

  • relocation would improve solar access to the property and/or adjoining properties,
  • the amenity of any adjoining residences would not be adversely impacted,
  • relocation will not impact on street trees, bus stops, bus zones, power lines and other services, on street parking, heritage values or the streetscape, and
  • relocation would not adversely impact the safety of motorists or pedestrians.

C4.2.5 The design and positioning of driveway crossings is to:

  • not result in the removal of, or damage to, existing street trees,
  • maintain the pattern of driveway crossover locations in the street and not result in a gap along the verge between any adjoining driveway of less than 6m, or greater than 3m , to prevent the creation of an undersized on-street parking space,
  • Where a driveway has to be relocated due to site constraints, and it is moved to a boundary where the neighbours driveway is located, one of the following two outcomes must be achieved:
  • Where the neighbour's driveway runs hard up against the boundary or is setback ≤500mm , the new driveway crossing is to remove the inside splay of the adjoining driveway and be constructed to provide a contiguous 6m wide driveway crossing that spans both the subject site and neighbouring site. This ensures undersized landscape verge spaces are not created and on -street parking is maximised,
  • Where the neighbour's driveway is setback from the property boundary >500mm, the proposed new driveway crossing location and design is to be setback enough to achieve a minimum 3m landscape area in the verge.
  • C4.2.6 Vehicle standing areas on common property within the front setback are not permitted.
  • C4.2.7 Vehicles accessing sites which front State roads shall be capable of entering and exiting in a forward direction (i.e. vehicle manoeuvring shall be fully maintained within the site).
  • C4.2.8 Vehicles accessing any shared parking area shall be capable of entering and exiting in a forward direction (i.e. vehicle manoeuvring shall be fully maintained within the site).
  • C4.2.9 Developments seeking additional driveway crossovers for developments with ≥2 dwellings, are subject to site constraints. Where a street tree or other site constraint is present, a dwelling may not be able to achieve on-site parking requirements. This may b e accepted by Council depending on the development type and location. Council may request an analysis of proximity to public transport, services and a high quality design that allows for active travel alternatives.

4.3 Pedestrian Access

C4.3.1 All developments must provide clear, well -defined and easily legible pedestrian access from the primary road to the front door or entry gate.

C4.3.2 Multi-Dwelling Housing Additional Requirements:

  • A minimum of one (1) dwelling must have direct frontage to the primary road and must be designed to incorporate private pedestrian access for that lot, and
  • For developments with a dwelling that does not have direct frontage to a public road, a common pedestrian access point, separate from the driveway, must be provided from the primary road. This access point must allow for access to all dwellings via a commo n pedestrian pathway that is integrated into the landscape design.
  • Any development proposing more than 4 dwellings that are on the same lot (strata) must have a common pedestrian access point and pathway from the primary road.
  • C4.3.3 Manor Homes are to have a common pedestrian entry point that leads to either an internal access path providing private dwelling access, or a common lobby. This is to be separated from vehicular access.
  • C4.3.4 Buildings with shared entry must ensure that the access point and or pathway to that access point is well defined and clearly identifiable from the public domain and any on -site communal open spaces.
  • C4.3.5 All pedestrian paths should form part of a cohesive landscape design.
  • C4.3.6 Ramping for accessibility should be minimised by building entry location and setting ground floor levels in relation to footpath levels. Ramping should be softened through forming an integrated part of the landscape design.

5. Private Open Space, Landscaping and Tree Planting

Objectives

O5.1 Maintain and enhance the landscaped characteristics of the locality.

  • O5.2 To achieve tree planting targets, prioritise retention of mature canopy trees through site planning and design.
  • O5.3 Provide for mature vegetation and the healthy growth of canopy trees, particularly large and medium sized trees in setbacks.
  • O5.4 Ensure a ll dwellings have access to usable private open space.
  • O5.5 Preserve and enhance native wildlife populations and habitat through appropriate planting of indigenous vegetation.
  • O5.6 Planting and landscaping is diverse and softens the visual impact of buildings.

Controls

C5.1 Landscaped Area

C5.1.1 Residential developments are to achieve the following landscaped areas:

Development TypeLot SizePercentage of the site area to be landscape area
Dwelling Houses Dual OccupanciesLots less than or equal to 750m²30%
Lots greater than 750m²35%
Multi-dwelling HousingLots less than 1,500m²25%
Terraces Manor HomesLots greater than or equal to 1,500m²30%

Landscaped area means a part of a site used for growing plants, grasses and trees, but does not include any building, structure or hard paved area.

Where multiple dwellings are proposed in a development, the landscape area is to be distributed evenly across the development site as much as practicably possible, ensuring all dwellings benefit from the amenity provided by the proposed landscape regime.

C5.1.2 Landscaping should be incorporated into the site planning of a development to:

  • Be suited to site conditions,
  • Maintain significant landscape features including established mature canopy trees,
  • Soften and improve the aesthetic quality of the development by planting a mix of lowlying shrubs, medium -high shrubs and canopy trees in locations where they will soften the built form,
  • Landscaped areas that are common property should enhance the visual amenity for surrounding dwellings and surrounding dwellings should provide passive surveillance of the space through bay windows, corner windows, patios and balconies ,
  • Ensure landscape design allows for distinction between common property areas and private open space, without compromising the amenity of either,
  • Provide opportunities for on-site stormwater infiltration.

C5.1.3 A Landscape Plan prepared by a suitably qualified landscape architect is to be submitted with all Development Applications for developments with ≥ 2 dwellings . For dwelling houses , a landscape plan must be submitted, but can be prepared by the architect/building designer or other suitably qualified person.

C5.1.4 Above ground landscaping on slabs and roofs, with a minimum dimension of 500mm may contribute to achieving the landscape area provision. Soil depth and volume must correspond with the proposed species and be considered in the submitted Landscape Drawings.

C5.1.5 Where landscaping is provided in a structured environment such as a raised planter box or 'on slab' they should include waterproofing, drainage and automatic irrigation and be shown on the submitted plans and supporting specifications .

C5.2 Deep Soil Area

C5.2.1 Residential developments are to achieve the following deep soil areas:

Development TypeLot SizePercentage of the site area to be deep soil area
Dwelling Houses Dual OccupanciesLots less than or equal to 750m²25%
Lots greater than 750m²30%
Multi-dwelling Housing Terraces Manor HomesLots less than 1,500m²20%
Lots greater than or equal to 1,500m²25%

*Note - Deep soil area is defined as any permeable surfaces located at ground level and provides areas for the growing of plants (including grasses, shrubs and trees) and areas with loose gravels or pebbles upon soil that water can easily penetrate. Deep soil area does not include any planted areas

above basements, podiums, roofs, slabs or areas located underneath covered structures.

C5.2.2 Any area included in the calculation of deep soil area must have a minimum dimension of 2m x 2m. The deep soil areas, including dimensions, are to be indicated on the Landscaping Plan submitted with the Development Application.

C5.2.3 Where pebbles or gravel are proposed instead of turf or soil garden beds, these spaces must feature soft landscaping embellishments or canopy trees.

C5.3 Front Setback Landscaping

C5.3.1 Dwelling Houses - minimum of 50% of the front building setback is to be deep soil area.

C5.3.2 Dual Occupancies, Multi Dwelling Housing, Terraces and Manor Homes - minimum of 40% of the front building setback is to be deep soil area.

C5.4 Private Open Space

C5.4.1 For Dwellings, Dual Occupancies, Multi -Dwelling Housing and Terraces, a n area of private open space is to be provided for each dwelling which:

  • Is located at ground level,
  • Is to be located at the rear of the dwelling and/or behind the building line established by the front setback,
  • Has a minimum dimension of 4m x 5m, which does not include any pool,
  • Is directly accessible from a main living area ,
  • May include a covered alfresco area.
  • C5.4.2 For Multi-Dwelling Housing developments, dwellings fronting the street may have the private open space within the front setback provided that:
  • Front fencing heights are complied with,
  • Landscaping is used to manage privacy and ensure passive surveillance of the street is achieved - A minimum 1m landscape buffer is required immediately inside the property boundary (either side of the proposed front fence),
  • Internal setbacks (between the front dwelling and any detached dwelling behind) are complied with.
  • C5.4.3 Private open space for Manor Homes must adjoin the main dwelling and achieve the following minimum areas:
  • Studio apartment - 4m² balcony,
  • 1 bedroom dwelling - 8m² balcony,
  • 2 bedroom dwelling - 10m² balcony,
  • 3+ bedroom dwelling - 12m² balcony,
  • For any proposed dwelling at ground level, a private open space area (such as a patio) is to be provided instead of a balcony. It must have a minimum area of 15m² and a minimum depth of 3m.

C5.4.4 Private open space for Manor Homes:

  • The minimum balcony dimension for the purposes of calculating the balcony area is 1 .5m,
  • The minimum area cannot be located adjoining the side setback (i.e it must be orientated towards the front or rear),
  • Additional area may be located adjoining the side setback (but not incorporate a structure that encroaches into the side setback) however must not be more than 1m in depth and incorporate suitable privacy mitigation measures,
  • Must adjoin living spaces ,
  • Storage areas do not count towards the minimum private open space size.
  • C5.4.5 All private open space is to be located to maximise solar access.
  • C5.4.6 All private open space is to be designed to minimise adverse impacts upon the privacy of the occupants of adjacent sites and within the proposed development
  • C5.4.7 All private open space must allow for landscaping and tree planting requirements to be met.

C5.5 Tree Canopy

C5.5.1 Site Planning and Design

  • Site planning and building design must prioritise retention of trees on site for the purposes of achieving tree planting targets set out in this section.
  • Retention of existing significant trees with mature canopy cover is the preferred means of achieving the tree planting requirements outlined in this section .

C5.5.2 Tree Planting Size Guide

Size categoryMin. diameter spreadMin. height
Small6m6-8m
Medium8m8-10m
Large12m10m+

C5.5.3 Tree Planting Requirements

New development or alterations and additions that incorporate changes to more than 50% of the site must achieve the following tree quantity, whether through retention of existing trees or new planting. Trees should be selected from Strathfield Council's selected tree specie s list.

Dwelling House and Dual Occupancies

  • For sites with an area 450-600m² - for every 200m² of site area or part thereof, a minimum of one (1) small tree located in the deep soil area,
  • For sites with an area >600m² - for every 225m² of site area or part thereof, a minimum of one (1) medium tree located in the deep soil area.

Multi-Dwelling Housing (Terraces)

  • For Multi-Dwelling Housing (Terraces) where the site area (being the Strata or Torrens Title boundary for that dwelling) is less than or equal to 300 m², a minimum of one small tree is required, located within the deep soil area,
  • For sites with an area > 300m², a minimum of one medium tree is required, located within a deep soil area,

Multi-Dwelling Housing & Manor Homes

  • For every 200m² or part thereof, a minimum of one medium tree is required, located within a deep soil area,

6. Fencing

Objectives

O6.1 Front fences allow for passive surveillance.

O6.1 Front fences allow for a soft transition between the public and private domain.

Controls

C6.1 Front Fencing

C6.1.1 Where a front fence is proposed, the fence is to be no higher than 1200mm. Front fences proposed at greater than 1200mm are to be supported by sufficient justification, including consistency with the streetscape and potential impacts on sight lines.

C6.1.2 Front fencing is to be located along the boundary line or setback no more than 1 000mm from the boundary line , with soft landscaping in between the fence and boundary. Details of the proposed landscaping within the setback are to be indicated on the Landscape Plans.

C6.1.3 Where a site is sloping along the front boundary, the front fence is to be designed to step with the slope of the site so that it is no more than 1.2m at any given point.

C6.1.4 Gates for secure access for pedestrians and vehicles are to be at or behind the front building line of the development. These gates should be integrated into the design and when built for at - grade access, should be no higher than 1.8m above the proposed gr ound level.

C6.2 Side and Rear Boundary Fencing

C6.2.1 Side and Rear boundary fencing is to be a maximum of 1.8m in height measured from existing ground level and constructed of timber of Colourbond. Masonry side and rear fences are permitted for corner allotments (along the street side) and for other boundaries of unique or irregular allotments and will be assessed on merit.

7. Solar Access

Objectives

O7.1 Design, site and modulate development to maximise solar access and sunlight from optimal directions into principal living spaces and private open spaces for the proposed dwellings.

O7.2 Minimise the loss of sunlight to the windows, principal living spaces and private open spaces of adjoining dwellings.

Controls

C7.1 Siting and Design

C7.1.1 Where a Design Verification Statement is required, it must address :

  • How the built form has been developed to maximise solar access into living spaces and private open space areas ,
  • How it has been designed to maximise solar access to the adjoining sites. Developments should modulate building mass and increase setbacks to allow for the solar access requirements to be achieved.

C7.2 Solar Access to Proposed Development

  • C7.2.1 For developments proposing ≤4 dwellings, 50% of the private open space and the principal living space of all dwellings must receive a minimum of 3 hours of direct sunlight between 8am and 4pm on 21 June (winter solstice).
  • C7.2.2 Where a development features >4 dwellings, 70% of the proposed dwellings must achieve the 50% solar access requirement in 7.2.1 above.

C7.2.3 Where Multi-dwelling Housing and Terrace d wellings are not achieving the 50% solar access requirement, those dwellings should feature upper -level passive balconies, small passive courtyards in the side and front setback and additional living spaces with northern exposure. These spaces must be suitably mana ged in terms of privacy and acoustic impacts to neighbouring properties.

C7.3 Solar Access to Neighbouring Properties

C7.3.1 Direct sunlight to all north facing windows of habitable rooms of adjacent dwellings should not be reduced to less than 3 hours between 8am and 4pm on 21 June (winter solstice). Where windows currently receive less than 3 hours, direct sunlight cannot be reduced.

  • C7.3.2 A minimum of 50% of the private open space of neighbouring dwellings must receive a minimum of 3 hours of direct sunlight between 8am and 4pm on 21 June. Consideration will be given to a reduction to this requirement where the neighbouring dwelling does not achieve 50% prior to development, in which case the solar access must not be reduced any further.
  • C7.3.3 Solar panels on neighbouring dwellings, which are situated not less than 6m above ground level (existing), must retain a minimum of 3 hours of direct sunlight between 8am and 4pm on 21 June.
  • C7.3.4 Where the neighbouring dwellings do not contain any solar panels, direct sunlight must be retained to the north, east and/or west roof planes of neighbouring dwellings, which are at least 6m above ground level (existing), so that future solar panels are a ble to capture 3 or more hours of sunlight between 8am and 4pm on 21 June.
  • C7.3.5 Any variation from the above requirements will be subject to a merit assessment having regard to the following factors:
  • Degree of meeting the FSR, height, setback and site coverage controls ,
  • Orientation of the subject site and adjoining allotments and subdivision pattern of the urban block,
  • Whether opportunities to increase side or rear setbacks have been considered,
  • Topography of the subject site and adjoining allotments ,
  • Use of increased setbacks to reduce shadow, especially along a southern boundary,
  • Whether the adjoining site being overshadowed has LEP development standards that allow for significant uplift (an increase in height or FSR of 100%).

C7.4 Shadow Diagram Requirements

C7.4.1 Shadow diagrams are to be submitted demonstrating the shadow impacts for the winter solstice (21 June) between 8am and 4pm.

C7.4.2 Shadow diagrams are required to show the impact of the proposal on solar access available to the living rooms and main open space of neighbouring properties. Existing overshadowing by fences, roof overhangs and changes in level should also be reflected in the diagrams. It may also be necessary to provide elevational or view from the sun diagrams to demonstrate appropriate solar access provision to adjoining dwellings, particularly where the allotment is oriented east - west

8. Visual Privacy and Acoustic Amenity

Objectives

O8.1 Development should minimise direct overlooking or cross-viewing into neighbouring dwellings.

O8.2 Upper-level balconies must be designed to provide privacy to both the residents of the development and minimise overlooking into neighbouring properties.

O8.3 Design and site development to minimise the intrusion of noise from external sources into habitable rooms, in particular bedrooms.

O8.4 Design and site development to minimise noise transmission between dwellings within the development and from the development to adjoining dwellings.

Controls

C8.1 Visual Privacy

C8.1.1 Development is to utilise site planning as the primary method for achieving visual and acoustic privacy. This may be realised through such measures as orientating living spaces to rear gardens or the street, collocating similar uses between dwellings, or p roviding greater separation to neighbouring sites. Ancillary measures such as screening should only be utilised where privacy cannot be achieved through site planning.

C8.1.2 Dwellings, Secondary Dwellings and Dual Occupancies - Balconies and terraces within the side setback are not permitted. This includes partly concealed courtyards at upper levels. Council will only consider balconies within the side setback where the side setback significantly exceeds the minimum requirements, and where the balcony will not impact on the privacy of neighbouring dwellings.

C8.1. 3 Multi-dwelling housing, Terraces and Manor Homes - Windows and balconies off main living areas should be directed towards the front and rear of the site as much as practically possible. Larger setbacks and privacy measures are required where developments have living spaces and private open spaces that are orientated towards a side boundary .

C8.1. 4 Windows and balconies of habitable rooms are not to directly overlook windows,

balconies and the open space of adjacent dwellings. To ensure appropriate privacy, consideration should be given to including:

  • Changes in the building line and building angles,
  • Physical screening devices such as louvres, shutters, window hoods and screens,
  • Splaying or staggering the location of windows,
  • Increasing building setbacks from the side boundary .

C8.1. 5 The use of tinted or opaque glazing as the sole means of achieving privacy along an entire facade is not permitted.

C8.1.6 Upper-level balconies must incorporate privacy measures that ensure overlooking is minimised. Privacy measures must be integrated into the design of the development. Suitable design responses include:

  • Solid and partially solid balustrades ,
  • Fin walls and privacy screens that form an integrated part of the dwelling design,
  • Recessed balconies and sunken levels,
  • Planters along the balcony edge.

C8.1.7 For Dwellings, Dual Occupancies, Multi -Dwelling Housing and Terraces, the maximum depth of an upper -level balcony in the rear setback is 2000mm. All upper level balconies for these development types must be located off bedrooms.

C8.1.8 Balconies and terraces within the side setback will generally not be supported. This includes partly concealed courtyards at upper levels. Council will consider balconies and terraces within the side setback for Manor Homes and MDH housing where:

  • the side setback significantly exceeds the minimum requirements and the portion of the balcony or terrace within the side setback is outside of the minimum area,
  • the balcony section within the side setback is located to achieve solar access requirements,
  • the section of balcony is less than 1000m in depth, has robust and well designed privacy mitigation elements and forms part of a balcony that is mostly orientated to the front or rear of the site,
  • the balcony or terrace will not impact on the privacy of neighbouring dwellings.

C8.1 .9 All balconies must be accessed internally. Council will not permit external stairs to access any upper-level balcony.

C8.1.10 Rooftop terraces are not permitted.

C8.1 .11 The floor level of alfresco and outdoor living areas at ground floor should be as close to existing ground level as possible and no higher than 1000mm from existing ground level . This may require stepping these spaces down from internal living areas where the neighbour's privacy is impacted and/or where privacy mitigation results in additional and avoidable bulk and scale.

C8.2 Acoustic Amenity

C8.2.1 Development is to be sited, designed and constructed to mirror the location of uses within each dwelling. Noisier spaces such as living rooms and alfresco areas should be located adjoining each other.

  • C8.2.2 Bedrooms, living spaces and other habitable rooms should be separated from any common gallery access and other open circulation space s.

C8.2.3 Noise generators such as air conditioning units, pool pumps and other plant or equipment are to be located away from windows or other openings in habitable rooms of the proposed dwellings and any adjoining dwellings . These are also to be screened or otherwise acoustically treated so plant and/or equipment do not emit a sound level that exceeds 5dB(A) above the ambient L90 background noise level at any property boundary.

C8.2.4 The Site Analysis and Design Verification Statement (when required) must identify potential sources of noise near the site and establish whether a noise impact assessment (prepared by a qualified engineer) is required.

C8.2.5 Where noise mitigation is required due to the sites position near a road, rail line, entertainment or industrial activities, child care centre or other noise emission - noise mitigation should form an integrated part of the development and not result in unarticulated facades or dwellings that require the majority (more than 50%) of windows and doors to be closed.

9. Dwelling Layout, Amenity and Safety

Objectives

O9.1 Provide habitable rooms that are of a size and design that is functional and provides a high standard of amenity for occupants.

O9.2 Ensure any common spaces are well landscaped and safe spaces.

O9.3 Provide a mix of dwelling types and sizes to accommodate a range of household types and to facilitate housing diversity.

O9.4 Ensure that dwellings achieve comfortable and accessible indoor environments for residents.

Controls

C9.1 Minimum Areas

C9.1.1 Developments are to achieve the following minimum internal areas:

  • Studio apartment - 35m²
  • 1 bedroom dwelling - 50m²
  • 2 bedroom dwelling - 70m²
  • 3+ bedroom dwelling - 90m²

The minimum internal areas include only one bathroom. Additional bathrooms increase the minimum internal area by 5m² each.

A fourth bedroom and further additional bedrooms increase the minimum internal area by 12m² each.

C9.1. 2 Every habitable room and at least one bathroom must have a window in an external wall with a total minimum glass area of not less than 10% of the floor area of the room. Daylight and air may not be borrowed from other rooms.

  • C9.1. 3 All bedrooms must have a minimum dimension of 3m. Master bedrooms are to have a minimum area of 10m², and all other bedrooms are to be a minimum of 9m² (excluding wardrobe space).
  • C9.1. 4 Living rooms or combined living/dining rooms have a minimum width of:
  • 3.6m for studio and 1 bedroom apartments ,
  • 4m for 2 and 3 + bedroom apartments.
  • C9.1.5 Any level in a dwelling that contains the principal living space is to have a floor to ceiling height of no less than 2.7m.

C9.2 Common / Communal Space Design Requirements

  • C9.2.1 Common open space, circulation areas (including lobby areas) are to avoid the creation of concealed spaces through passive surveillance opportunities and clear site lines.
  • C9.2.2 Landscaping must be used to balance safety with aesthetics.
  • C9.2.3 D evelopment with ≥ 6 dwellings are to include an assessment demonstrating compliance against the Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED)'s Safer by Design Guidelines .
  • C9.2.4 Lighting is to be shown on the Architectural Drawings. Lighting details must demonstrate enhanced visibility and safety perception, and minimi sed glare and light spill age.

C9.3 Dwelling Mix

  • C9.3.1 Developments with >4 dwellings are to achieve the following dwelling mix:
  • No more than 25% of the dwelling yield is to comprise either studio or one bedroom dwellings.
  • No less than 20% of the dwelling yield is to comprise dwellings with three or more bedrooms.
  • C9.3.2 25% of dwellings proposed in a development with ≥4 dwellings must achieve the Liveable Housing Guideline's silver level universal design features

C9.4 Cross Ventilation

  • All apartments/dwellings are to be naturally cross ventilated. Apartments are designed to minimise the number of corners, doors and rooms that might obstruct airflow. Apartment depths, combined with appropriate ceiling heights, maximise cross ventilation and airflow

10. Materials and Finishes

Objectives

O10.1 External materials, colour schemes and building details reinforce and enhance identifiable material characteristics in the street and locality.

Controls

C10.1.1 External materials and colours should be sympathetic to the streetscape and make a positive contribution to the overall appearance of the building.

C10.1.1 Materials and finishes across a development and/or site should achieve a cohesive outcome.

C10.1. 2 Materials and finishes should have low reflectivity. Extensive use of highly reflective materials will not be permitted for roof or wall cladding. Large and unarticulated expansive surfaces of predominantly white or light render or primary colours that would dominate the streetscape will not be supported.

C10.1. 3 Materials should be durable and require minimal façade maintenance.

C10.1. 4 Downpipes, air-conditioning units and other plant are to be hidden from view on the front façade or integrated into the design.

11. Site Facilities, Services and Ancillary Structures

Objectives

O11.1 Adequate provision is made for site facilities to support residential occupation of the development.

O11.2 Services and ancillary structures do not detract from the amenity of the public domain or neighbouring sites.

O11.3 Site utilities are accessible, visually unobtrusive and require minimal maintenance.

Controls

C11.1 Site Facilities and Services

C11.1.1 All dwellings are to be provided with adequate and practical external storage . The minimums are as follows:

  • Studio apartment - 4m³
  • 1 bedroom dwelling - 6m³
  • 2 bedroom dwelling - 8m³
  • 3+ bedroom dwelling - 10m³

These storage spaces are to be located near to the allocated parking spaces for each dwelling.

C11.1. 2 Secure and undercover storage for bicycles and other outdoor equipment should be provided, whether communal or as part of storage provision requirements in (a) -(d) above.

C11.1. 3 External storage spaces should be screened and integrated with the building design .

C11.1. 4 Fixed clothes drying spaces in private open spaces and communal open spaces should not be visible from the public domain and be located in areas with good exposure to natural light.

C11.1. 5 Letterboxes are to be located on the frontage where the address has been allocated in accordance with Australia Post requirements. Parcel drop areas should be considered for developments where shared entry points are proposed.

C11.1. 6 Appliances and services such as air conditioning units must be concealed in customised storage spaces that are integrated into the building design when located in the front setback or if visible from the public domain.

C11.1. 7 Minimise visual impact of solar systems by:

  • Using a colour that is consistent with the colour of roof materials,
  • Designing solar panels, where possible, as part of the roof ,
  • Setting the solar panels back from the street frontage and position below the ridgeline ,

C11.1. 8 Fire hydrants and any plant or servicing equipment and structures are to be shown on all architectural drawings. These elements must be integrated into the building and/or landscape design and must not create a dominating element in the front façade or front setback area (including along the fence line).

C11.2 Swimming Pools

C11 .2.1 Swimming pools must be located within the rear setback and form part of a cohesive landscape design strategy. Details of the swimming pools are to be included on the architectural and landscape plans submitted with the D evelopment Application. Swimming pools within the side setback to a secondary street are permitted, subject to compliance with other appliable development controls.

C11 .2.2 The swimming pool water line must be setback a minimum of 1 000mm from any side or rear boundary.

C11 .2.3 Decking and paving around a swimming pool must not be more than 250mm above existing ground level.

C11 .2.4 The pool must be designed to ensure the boundary fence is not needed to extend beyond 1.8m in height from existing ground level.

C11 .3 Outbuildings

C11 .3.1 Any outbuilding is to be located within the rear setback.

  • C11.3.2 The size of any outbuilding must not impact on the delivery of minimum landscape and deep soil area requirements across a site.

C11 .3.3 The maximum height of any outbuilding is 3.5m from existing ground level.

C11 .3.4 The minimum setback is 9 00mm from the side and the rear boundary.

C11 .3.5 Where an allotment has access via a rear lane, the outbuilding may have a nil rear setback and a maximum height of 6m.

C11 .4 Tennis Courts

C11 .4.1 Tennis courts are to be sited at the rear of properties.

C11. 4.2 Tennis court fences must comply with the applicable side setback controls and must be setback a minimum of 3m from any rear boundary with landscaping between the boundary and tennis court fence.

C11 .4.3 Tennis courts must not compromise delivery of minimum landscape and deep soil area controls, as well as cut and fill requirements.

C11 .5 Carports

C11 .5.1 Carports must be a maximum of 3m in height and located behind the front building line.

C11 .5.2 Carports must be setback 0.5m from the side boundary and open on at least two sides (front and side or front and back).

12. Development on Corner Sites & Adjoining Open Space

Objectives

O12 .1 Ensure that development on corner allotments appropriately address the primary street and secondary street.

O12 .2 Design and orientate development (access, private open space , landscaping etc) on corner allotments to minimise adverse amenity impacts for neighbouring dwellings.

Controls

C12.1 Siting and Setbacks

  • C12.1 .1 For two storey developments orientated towards the primary road, the secondary street side setback is 3m. Any third storey must be setback an additional 1.5m.
  • C12.1. 2 Any new dwelling fronting the secondary street must achieve the front setback requirements under section 3 of this DCP.
  • C12.1. 3 Where a site or new allotment has a rear boundary adjoining the side boundary of a neighbouring allotment, the minimum rear setback is 6m.

C12.2 Access

  • C12.2.1 Designing vehicular access to the development, and whether it is achieved via the primary or secondary road, should be informed by the frontage with the least existing constraints (location of street trees, pedestrian thoroughfares and narrow allotments or splays) .
  • C12.2.2 For dwellings fronting the secondary street, appropriate pedestrian access is to be provided from the secondary street frontage, and the design of the access must be integrated as part of the overall design of the development.

C12.3 Articulation

C12.3.1 Any side elevation to the secondary street must be articulated to address the street and achieve passive surveillance.

C12.4 Private Open Space

C12.4.1 A principal private open space area is to be located behind the front building line of the dwelling facing the secondary setback. The design and location of private open space must incorporate appropriate privacy mitigation measures where the lot configuration results in unusual proximity to neighbouring living spaces and rear y ards.

C12.5 Secondary Street Fencing

C12.5.1 Where a Dwelling, Dual Occupancy, or side of a Terrace (but not the rear) development is siding onto a secondary street, a 1.8m high fence is permitted along part of the secondary street boundary. The solid component must be integrated into the front fence and must only start behind the front setback to the primary street/road.

C12.5.2 Parks and open space

Where development adjoins public parks, open space or bushland, the design must positively address this interface and use a number of the following design solutions:

  • street access, pedestrian paths and building entries which are clearly defined ,
  • paths, low fences and planting that clearly delineate between communal/private open space and the adjoining public open space ,
  • minimal use of blank walls and fences.

13. Secondary Dwellings

Explanatory Note - This section provides controls for secondary dwellings. These controls are in addition to the controls in sections above.

Objectives

O1 3.1 Secondary dwellings are designed with regard to the site constraints and opportunities.

O1 3.2 To ensure that a secondary dwelling does not compromise the principal dwellings compliance with the applicable development standards and controls.

O1 3.3 To ensure that secondary dwellings do not unreasonably impact on the amenity of adjoining sites.

Controls

C13.1 Location

C13.1.1 Where a secondary dwelling is being attached to or incorporated into the building envelope of a new dwelling, or where part of an existing dwelling is being converted into a secondary dwelling, the secondary dwelling and principal dwelling must comply with the height and setback requirements for single dwellings.

C13.1.2 Detached secondary dwellings are to be located behind the rear building line of the primary dwelling.

C13.2 Setbacks

Detached secondary dwellings should be setback as follows:

  • 3m from the rear boundary unless the site has access to a rear laneway, in which case the secondary dwelling can have a nil setback,
  • 1500mm from any side boundary,
  • Detached secondary dwellings must be a minimum of 6m from the wall of the primary dwelling.

C13.3 Building height

  • C13.3.1 Detached secondary dwellings are to be single storey only.
  • C13.3.2 Basements are not permitted as part of a detached secondary dwelling .
  • C13.3.3 For a pitched roof outcome, the secondary dwelling may incorporate an attic space that complies with the attic controls and objectives in this section of the DCP,
  • C13.3.4 Detached secondary dwellings above a garage, located with frontage to a rear lane , are permitted to be two storeys in total (inclusive of garage).

C13.4 Access and Parking

C13.4.1 The secondary dwelling is to have an identifiable pedestrian entry point.

C13.4.1 Refer to Traffic and Parking controls for parking and access requirements.

C13. 5 Landscaping, Deep Soil and Private Open Space

  • C13. 5.1 The secondary dwelling must ensure that the minimum landscape and deep soil areas required for the principal dwelling can be complied with.
  • C13. 5.2 Secondary dwellings must be provided with a primary private open space area directly accessible to the internal living areas of the dwelling. The private open space area should:
  • have an area of 6m² and minimum dimension of 1m².
  • have some separation, in either distance or by landscaping embellishment, from the principal dwelling,
  • May include a deck that is not more than 500mm above existing ground level.

C13. 6 Privacy

C13. 6.1 Obscured glazing should be minimised. Privacy should be managed through site planning, orientation, architectural design, landscaping and screens integrated into the dwelling design.

C13. 7 Solar Access

C13. 7.1 Secondary dwellings should be designed to maximise light into living spaces and private open space areas. This must be balanced with the protection of solar access for neighbouring dwellings and the primary dwelling.

STRATHFIELD MUNICIPAL COUNCIL

PART D of Strathfield Consolidated Development Control Plan

Industrial Development

(Replaces DCP No. 27)

2.2 Contamination

Objective:

To ensure that a site is safe for development or redevelopment.

Guidelines:

Under State Environmental Planning Policy (SEPP) No. 55 - Remediation of Land, Council cannot consent to the carrying out of any development on land unless:

  • It has considered whether the land is contaminated, and
  • If the land is contaminated, it is satisfied that the land is suitable in its contaminated state (or will be suitable, after remediation) for the purposes for which the development is proposed to be carried out, and
  • If the land requires remediation to be made suitable for the purpose for which the development is proposed to be carried out, it is satisfied that the land will be remediated before the land is used for that purpose.

To ensure that a development application is appropriately assessed by Council under the requirements of SEPP 55, where an industrial development is proposed on a site that is identified as potentially unhealthy or contaminated, a preliminary investigation may be required to be submitted to Council by the applicant to demonstrate that the site is safe for development.

Where an environmental site contamination assessment is required to be produced to Council, the assessment must take into consideration the Department of Planning and the Environment Protection Authority's (EPA) document Managing Land Contamination Planning Guidelines SEPP 55 - Remediation of Land, 1998 . Some activities that may cause or may have caused contamination are identified in that document.

Please Note:

  • Under the Contaminated Land Management Act 1997 and the Duty to Report provision in relation to contaminated land, where Council becomes aware of a site that has been contaminated or potentially contaminated and there is a significant risk of off-site harm, Council must notify the EPA in writing that the land has been contaminated or is potentially contaminated.
  • Council has a Policy for the Management of Development on Contaminated Land which includes Part K - Development on Contaminated Land. This document should be referred to if the subject site is contaminated or potentially contaminated.

2.3 Subdivision

Objective:

To ensure subdivision results in lots that are suitable for a range of industrial developments.

2.5 Density, Bulk and Scale

Height, Floor Space Ratio and Office and Showroom Requirements

Objective:

To ensure the density, bulk, scale and design of industrial development enhances the streetscape and visual quality of the Strathfield Municipality.

Guidelines and Requirements:

2.5.1 Height

A building shall not have a wall height of more than 10m above natural ground level. Where an industrial development otherwise achieves the objectives of Part D, Council may consider varying this provision depending on the merits of the case.

2.5.2 Floor Space Ratio

The maximum floor space ratio is 1:1.

2.5.3 Office and Showroom Requirements

  • All office and showroom activities shall be ancillary to the main industrial activity approved for the site.
  • Proposals which include a large area dedicated to office or showroom purposes (in excess of 25%) will need to be substantiated by evidence that the location is necessary because either no suitable business zoned land is available, or that the use is of a type that location in a business zone is not desirable.

2.6 Setbacks

Objectives:

  • To ensure setbacks for industrial buildings provide adequate space for landscaping to soften the built form and enhance the amenity of the streetscape;
  • To ensure setbacks from watercourses and bushland are adequate to provide protection to those areas and an opportunity for the restoration/establishment of native vegetation;
  • To reduce the visual and/or acoustic impacts of industrial development on surrounding non-industrial land uses; and
  • To ensure frontage setbacks are consistent with surrounding industrial development.

Guidelines and Requirements:

  • A minimum setback of 10m from the front boundary applies.
  • On corner lots, a setback of 5m applies to the secondary frontage.
  • A minimum 10m setback will be required from watercourses (eg Cooks River and Coxs Creek) and bushland. The Department of Infrastructure Planning and Natural Resources (formerly known as the Department of Land and Water Conservation) may require a greater setback from watercourses and consent may jointly be required from them and Council (Integrated Development). Contact should be made with them early if development is planned in the vicinity of a watercourse.
  • If nearby existing industrial buildings have setbacks less than the above, a variation on setback requirements may be considered.
  • Side and rear boundary setbacks for proposals adjoining non-industrial uses such as residential development shall be subject to an individual merit based assessment. Such an assessment will consider issues such as privacy, solar access, and visual and acoustic amenity.
  • Side and rear boundaries adjoining industrial development may not require a setback; this will depend on the individual situation.
  • Setbacks shall not contain any buildings or storage areas but may contain car parking and manoeuvring areas (and landscaping).
  • Refer to Section 2.10.6 - 2.10.9 for landscaping requirements within setbacks.

2.7 Building Requirements and Materials

Objectives:

  • To ensure that industrial development is of a high standard of design and appearance so as to contribute to the enhancement of the Strathfield Municipality;
  • To encourage innovative industrial development within the Strathfield Municipality; and
  • To encourage design and building materials that complement and enhance the surrounding environment.

Guidelines and Requirements:

  • Front walls and walls visible from any public place shall be substantially faced with brick, stone, concrete, glass (non-reflective) or like materials, but not cement render.
  • Walls/surfaces that are easily accessible to public places are to be treated (eg screened by plants) to discourage graffiti.
  • No service plumbing or pipes, other than downpipes for the conveyance of roof water, shall be external to the building where visible from any public place.
  • Long blank walls on street frontages are to be avoided. Where this is not possible, they are to be screened by appropriate landscaping or incorporate design features into the walls.
  • On corner sites, the proposed building shall aim to address both frontages. Where the secondary frontage cannot also be addressed, suitable landscaping is to be proposed (see section 2.10.6) and/or design features incorporated into the wall.
  • Building materials and colours used on facades facing the street shall be compatible with those of adjoining industrial buildings.
  • Non-industrial aspects of the development, ie offices or showrooms ancillary to the development, shall face the street.
  • Buildings must be designed to:
  • Architecturally express the structure of the building (not hiding behind expansive glass).
  • Visually reinforce entrances, office components and stairwells of units to create rhythm on long facades and a reduction of perceived scale.
  • Introduce variation in unit design within building groups;
  • Introduce solid surfaces, preferably masonry, incorporate horizontal and vertical modulation including windows in appropriate proportions and configurations.
  • Achieve a balance between masonry (or materials and solid panels that reflect masonry materials) and vertical walling which contain large areas of glass. Solid surfaces of rendered and painted masonry should dominate the overall building facade. Where glazing is used, it is to be modulated with vertical or horizontal members (mullions) between the lights of a window to provide visually recognisable patterns, rhythm and texture to the overall design. Such glazing is to be non-reflective.
  • Applicants will be required to indicate on development application plans building materials and colours proposed.

2.8 Energy Efficiency and Water Conservation

Objectives:

  • To orientate buildings so they maximise the use of solar energy to keep buildings cool in summer and warm in winter;
  • To encourage the use of building materials that assist in achieving energy efficient buildings;
  • To conserve water and reduce stormwater by the use of rainwater tanks and AAA rated water saving appliances and fittings;
  • To encourage the use of energy efficient appliances and fittings and where possible the use of renewable energy sources to reduce greenhouse gas emissions; and
  • To encourage the use of recycled building materials where appropriate.

Guidelines and Requirements:

  • New buildings are to be orientated as much as possible so that they make best use of solar energy to lower heating and cooling costs.
  • Glazing on north facing facades is encouraged to maximise solar access in winter and glazing to the west is to be minimised to reduce summer solar access.
  • Building materials and insulation are to be used which assist in thermal performance and maintain internal comfort levels of a building.
  • A rainwater tank must be included in all industrial developments to be used for landscape watering and other supplies of non-domestic water (ie toilets and machinery). The size of the tank(s) required will be based on 10 litres/m 2 of roof area proposed. Automatic landscape irrigation systems shall be connected to and utilise the rainwater tank. A tank or tanks with a total volume of up to 10,000 litres can be installed without consent, see Appendix 3 for installation guidelines.
  • Developments are required to be fitted with appliances and plumbing hardware which have a 'AAA' Australian Standards Water Conservation Rating and meet the manual of Assessment Procedure for Water Efficient Appliances SAA MP64-1995 which aim to reduce water consumption.
  • Any hot water heaters to be installed are to be greenhouse gas friendly systems that achieve a minimum 3.5 SEDA Hot Water Greenhouse Score. Systems which comply with this requirement are outlined in Figure 2.
  • The use of top star rated energy smart appliances and lighting is required. The Label Star Energy Rating System gives a rating to a range of appliances based on their energy efficiency. The more stars you see, the more efficient the model. Energy Smart light includes the use of fluorescent and compact fluorescent globes, self timing systems, dimmers, motion sensors and specific purpose switches.
  • All external lighting and common areas (eg undercover car parking) are required to be lit utilising renewable energy resources generated on site. Larger developments (buildings exceeding 4,000m 2 in area) must investigate the viability of utilising renewable energy resources for all lighting on site and a statement included with the development application addressing this requirement for the consideration of Council.
